See, my cousin has been needing a lot of help recently, and there’s a whole lot of logistics to sort out with his schedule. So my wife will be sitting right across from me, maybe at the kitchen table while we're having our morning coffee, and she’ll be telling me all the details about my cousin’s upcoming appointments, or who is supposed to be giving him rides on what day—you know, really important stuff that we need to keep track of. We’ve known each other for years, probably since our kids were in Little League together. And Bob was telling me this whole story about his daughter’s new house and the plumbing issues they were having. He was getting really into the details about the pipes and the water pressure, and I was standing right there, leaning on the counter, looking right at him. I was even saying \"uh-huh\" and \"wow, that's rough\" at all the right times. Well, yes, it really is, and that’s the part that really gets to me the most, honestly. I mean, it’s definitely spilling over into everything else. 

Take the situation with my wife, for example. I know I mentioned my cousin earlier, the one we help out. I want to be a partner she can rely on, especially at our age, but when she asks me to handle a piece of his schedule and the information just completely vanishes from my head... well, I can entirely see why she's at her wit's end with me. 

And then, outside of the house, it's making my daily activities so much harder than they used to be. Like I was saying about the volunteer work at St. Jude's and those catering orders. Because I can't seem to hold onto the information when I'm reading the menus or listening to the planning committee, I'm finding that I have to constantly double-check absolutely everything I do. I mean, I'll spend twenty extra minutes re-reading a simple catering sheet just to make absolutely sure I didn't mix up the small jobs. The other day, I almost ordered fifty paper tablecloths instead of the heavy-duty plastic ones because I just wasn't retaining what the event coordinator had told me on the phone. I caught it, thank goodness, but I had to tear up the form and redo the whole order. 

So, yeah, I’m always having to go back and double-check or completely redo these catering tasks just so things don't get mixed up for the parish events. It's exhausting, to tell you the truth. It makes me feel like I can't trust my own brain, having to second-guess myself all day long just to make sure I'm not ruining the summer festival or letting my wife down.

Physical sensation? You know, doctor, I’ve never really stopped to think about it quite like that. That’s a fascinating way to look at it, actually. Because, well, you hear about people who get, I don't know, a tension headache when they can't concentrate, or they get all jittery and restless in their legs. My brother-in-law, actually, whenever he gets overwhelmed or stops paying attention, he gets this very noticeable twitch right under his left eye. You can always tell when he's checked out of a conversation because that eye just starts going a mile a minute. 

But for me? No. No, there's absolutely nothing physical that happens. There’s no warning bell, no tingling, no heavy feeling in my head. Nothing like that at all. I could just be sitting in my La-Z-Boy—I’ve got this old brown leather recliner in the den, had it for maybe fifteen years, it's perfectly broken in right exactly to my shape—and I’ll be sitting there reading the parish bulletin or looking over those catering sheets for the church. Physically, I feel completely fine. Comfortable, relaxed, maybe holding my coffee mug. My body is just doing exactly what it's supposed to do. 

It’s almost insidious, really, when you think about it. Because if there *was* some kind of physical feeling—like, say, a little buzz in my ears or a pinch in my neck—then maybe I’d have a warning! I could catch myself and say, 'Oh, there goes my brain again, better snap back to the menu.' But because it’s completely silent, I don't even realize it's happening. One second I'm reading about the St. Jude's bake sale, feeling totally normal, and the next second my body is still sitting there feeling totally normal, but my mind is a million miles away, trying to remember if I put the cap back on the weed wacker gas can in the garage. So, no, I don't feel a single thing in my body. It's purely just my brain quietly sneaking out the back door without making a sound.

Well, no, not at all. My memory for the past is actually sharp as a tack. It’s funny you ask that, because my wife and I were just talking about this the other day. I can remember things from twenty, thirty, forty years ago with absolute perfect clarity. It's just the stuff right in front of me right now that vanishes. 

Like, I can tell you all about the year we bought our first house. Nineteen eighty-five, over on Elm Street. It was this little ranch-style place, had this horrible, bright yellow wallpaper in the kitchen—I mean, just a complete eyesore, looked like a giant canary had exploded in there. I spent three whole weekends, maybe four, scraping that stuff off the walls with a cheap putty knife and a spray bottle of warm water and vinegar. I remember my hands were blistered for a week, and the smell of that old glue... I can still smell it if I think about it. And I remember all the guys I used to work with before I retired, too. Their names, their kids' names, who drove what car. Jimmy Henderson drove this beat-up old blue Ford pickup that backfired every single time he pulled into the lot at 6:45 in the morning. Woke up half the neighborhood, I swear. 

So, yeah, everything from back then, long before I started getting so... well, scatterbrained with my reading and my conversations... all of those old memories are perfectly intact. Locked in there tight. I could probably draw you a map of my elementary school right now if you asked me to, down to exactly where the water fountains were in the second-grade hallway. It’s really just the present moment, you know? The right-now kind of information, the catering sheets and the schedules, that just slips right through the cracks like water through a sieve. But the past? No, the past is clear as a bell. I was just telling my wife about our road trip to the Grand Canyon back in '92, and I remembered the exact name of the diner we stopped at in Flagstaff—Route 66 Diner, had a red neon sign with a missing 'R' so it just said 'oute 66'. She couldn't believe I remembered that. So, no, absolutely no issues with the older memories whatsoever. It's just the new stuff that just refuses to stick in my head.

Emotionally? Gosh, you know, I’m really not sure how to answer that. I haven't really stopped to take my emotional temperature, so to speak, when it happens. I mean, I know how it makes my wife feel—she gets upset and frustrated, like I was saying before—but for me, in that exact moment when I realize my brain just took a little vacation? I don't know if I feel much of anything, emotionally speaking. 

Like, let's say I'm looking at the St. Jude's parish newsletter. We get it every Thursday in the mail, usually right around 11 o'clock when the regular mailman, Gary, comes by. Nice guy, Gary, he always leaves a little milk bone for the neighbor's golden retriever on his route. Anyway, I'll be sitting there in my recliner, reading the front page about the upcoming bake sale or the youth group car wash, and suddenly I realize I've been staring at the word 'cupcake' for five minutes and I haven't absorbed a single sentence of the actual article. 

When that happens, I don't get mad, I don't get sad or anything like that. I just sort of blink and think, 'Well, there I go again.' It's more of a... I don't know, a mechanical reset, I guess? I just go back to the top of the page and try again. I really don't have a big emotional reaction to it. 

I suppose maybe I feel a tiny bit foolish or embarrassed if I'm actually talking to someone face-to-face. Like if I'm talking to Father Thomas down at the church, and I have to ask him to repeat what he just said about setting up the folding chairs for the third time. He's a busy man, he's got a whole congregation to run, he doesn't have time to repeat himself. But even then, it's just a quick, 'Oops, sorry Father, lost my train of thought.' I don't go home and beat myself up over it or get all depressed or anything. So, yeah, emotionally... I'd have to say I don't really notice any strong feelings one way or the other. I just kind of shrug it off, apologize if I need to, and try to force myself to pay better attention the second time around.

Learn new things? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, if anything, I think I pick up on new things just as well as I did when I was thirty. 

Just last month, for instance, my daughter Sarah—she lives out in Denver now, works for a logistics company out there, doing very well for herself—she sent me one of those fancy wood pellet smokers for my birthday. It's one of those big heavy ones with the digital thermostats and the Wi-Fi connection built right into the hopper. Now, I have been a charcoal man my entire life. Just standard briquettes, a metal chimney starter, and maybe some soaked hickory chips if I was feeling ambitious on a holiday weekend. So this whole electronic, computerized smoker thing was completely new territory for me. 

But I tell you what, I figured it out without a hitch. I tried reading the manual at first, though naturally my mind wandered off a few times just like we were talking about earlier, but then I went on the computer and found these instructional videos. There is this fella on there from Texas who explains the whole setup process. I had to learn how to prime the auger, how to clear out the fire pot, and how to pair the grill's computer to the internet router in the house. Which, let me tell you, our router is all the way in the front office, so I actually had to go down to the electronics store and buy a signal extender just to get the Wi-Fi to reach out to the back patio. I ended up plugging it into the outlet right behind my wife's rhododendrons. 

Anyway, I learned that entire system in a single afternoon. I smoked a nine-pound pork shoulder the very next day. Fourteen hours at 225 degrees, used a mix of apple and cherry wood pellets, and it came out absolutely perfect. The meat just fell right off the bone. Even my wife, who usually doesn't care for heavy barbecue, went back for a second sandwich. 

So, no, the actual learning part is completely fine. Comprehending how a new piece of machinery works, or picking up a new skill, or even figuring out the new spreadsheet software they started using for the church finances—that hasn't changed a bit. My brain is perfectly capable of grasping new concepts and holding onto them once I actually get into the rhythm of doing it. It really is just that drifting issue, the part where I just stop absorbing the words right in front of me. But if you are asking if my overall ability to learn has gone downhill, I would have to give you a firm no on that one. I can still learn anything I set my mind to.

Oh, heavens no. No, not at all. The routines are... well, they're practically baked into my bones at this point. I don't have any trouble remembering how to do the things I've always done. 

Take the lawn care, for instance. I’ve got a quarter-acre lot, mostly Bermuda grass, which, let me tell you, can be a real nightmare if you don't stay right on top of it. I’ve been mowing that exact same lawn since we moved in. Every Tuesday morning, 8:00 AM sharp—well, unless it’s raining, of course, or if the morning dew is still too heavy, because you never want to cut wet grass, it just clumps up terribly and dulls the blade. But I go out to the shed, I pull out my Toro push mower. It’s a Recycler series, 22-inch deck, going on twelve years old now, and I know exactly how to maintain it without a second thought. I know it takes exactly 18 ounces of SAE 30 motor oil, I know to pop off the spark plug wire before I tip it over, and I know to use this old wooden paint stirrer I keep on the top shelf to scrape the dried clippings out from under the deck so the metal doesn't rust. It's just muscle memory. I could probably do the whole maintenance routine blindfolded. 

And it’s the exact same way with my hobbies. I tie my own flies for fly fishing, have since I took a class at the community college back in my twenties. Now, tying a Parachute Adams or an Elk Hair Caddis, that requires remembering a very specific, delicate sequence of steps. You have to wrap the thread, tie in the tail, dub the body, wrap the hackle... it’s a whole intricate process. But when I sit down at my vise down in the basement—I have this little corner set up next to the water heater with a nice daylight lamp—my hands just know exactly what to do. I don't need to look at a manual or pull up one of those internet videos I mentioned earlier. The knowledge is just right there, ready to go. 

So, no, I never walk up to the washing machine and forget which cycle to use, or sit down at my workbench and forget how to operate my tools. The everyday chores and the old hobbies are completely untouched. Like I was saying, it really just boils down to that one specific problem of my brain drifting off when I'm trying to take in something right in front of me, like a conversation or a newspaper article. But the established routines? No, they're solid as a rock.

I could just be sitting in my La-Z-Boy—I’ve got this old brown leather recliner in the den, had it for maybe fifteen years, it's perfectly broken in right exactly to my shape—and I’ll be sitting there reading the parish bulletin or looking over those catering sheets for the church. Physically, I feel completely fine. Comfortable, relaxed, maybe holding my coffee mug. My body is just doing exactly what it's supposed to do. \n\nIt’s almost insidious, really, when you think about it. Because if there *was* some kind of physical feeling—like, say, a little buzz in my ears or a pinch in my neck—then maybe I’d have a warning! I could catch myself and say, 'Oh, there goes my brain again, better snap back to the menu.' But because it’s completely silent, I don't even realize it's happening. One second I'm reading about the St. Jude's bake sale, feeling totally normal, and the next second my body is still sitting there feeling totally normal, but my mind is a million miles away, trying to remember if I put the cap back on the weed wacker gas can in the garage. So, no, I don't feel a single thing in my body. It's purely just my brain quietly sneaking out the back door without making a sound.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble remembering things that happened before this issue with absorbing information started?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not at all. My memory for the past is actually sharp as a tack. It’s funny you ask that, because my wife and I were just talking about this the other day. I can remember things from twenty, thirty, forty years ago with absolute perfect clarity. It's just the stuff right in front of me right now that vanishes. \n\nLike, I can tell you all about the year we bought our first house. Nineteen eighty-five, over on Elm Street. It was this little ranch-style place, had this horrible, bright yellow wallpaper in the kitchen—I mean, just a complete eyesore, looked like a giant canary had exploded in there. I spent three whole weekends, maybe four, scraping that stuff off the walls with a cheap putty knife and a spray bottle of warm water and vinegar. I remember my hands were blistered for a week, and the smell of that old glue... I can still smell it if I think about it. And I remember all the guys I used to work with before I retired, too. Their names, their kids' names, who drove what car. Jimmy Henderson drove this beat-up old blue Ford pickup that backfired every single time he pulled into the lot at 6:45 in the morning. Woke up half the neighborhood, I swear. \n\nSo, yeah, everything from back then, long before I started getting so... well, scatterbrained with my reading and my conversations... all of those old memories are perfectly intact. Locked in there tight. I could probably draw you a map of my elementary school right now if you asked me to, down to exactly where the water fountains were in the second-grade hallway. It’s really just the present moment, you know? The right-now kind of information, the catering sheets and the schedules, that just slips right through the cracks like water through a sieve. But the past? No, the past is clear as a bell. I was just telling my wife about our road trip to the Grand Canyon back in '92, and I remembered the exact name of the diner we stopped at in Flagstaff—Route 66 Diner, had a red neon sign with a missing 'R' so it just said 'oute 66'. She couldn't believe I remembered that. So, no, absolutely no issues with the older memories whatsoever. It's just the new stuff that just refuses to stick in my head.\n\nDoctor: How do you feel emotionally when you realize you haven't taken in what someone was saying or what you were reading?\n\nPatient: Emotionally? Gosh, you know, I’m really not sure how to answer that. I haven't really stopped to take my emotional temperature, so to speak, when it happens. I mean, I know how it makes my wife feel—she gets upset and frustrated, like I was saying before—but for me, in that exact moment when I realize my brain just took a little vacation? I don't know if I feel much of anything, emotionally speaking. \n\nLike, let's say I'm looking at the St. Jude's parish newsletter. We get it every Thursday in the mail, usually right around 11 o'clock when the regular mailman, Gary, comes by. Nice guy, Gary, he always leaves a little milk bone for the neighbor's golden retriever on his route. Anyway, I'll be sitting there in my recliner, reading the front page about the upcoming bake sale or the youth group car wash, and suddenly I realize I've been staring at the word 'cupcake' for five minutes and I haven't absorbed a single sentence of the actual article. \n\nWhen that happens, I don't get mad, I don't get sad or anything like that. I just sort of blink and think, 'Well, there I go again.' It's more of a... I don't know, a mechanical reset, I guess? I just go back to the top of the page and try again. I really don't have a big emotional reaction to it. \n\nI suppose maybe I feel a tiny bit foolish or embarrassed if I'm actually talking to someone face-to-face. Like if I'm talking to Father Thomas down at the church, and I have to ask him to repeat what he just said about setting up the folding chairs for the third time. He's a busy man, he's got a whole congregation to run, he doesn't have time to repeat himself. But even then, it's just a quick, 'Oops, sorry Father, lost my train of thought.' I don't go home and beat myself up over it or get all depressed or anything. So, yeah, emotionally... I'd have to say I don't really notice any strong feelings one way or the other. I just kind of shrug it off, apologize if I need to, and try to force myself to pay better attention the second time around.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it harder to learn new things than you used to?\n\nPatient: Learn new things? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, if anything, I think I pick up on new things just as well as I did when I was thirty. \n\nJust last month, for instance, my daughter Sarah—she lives out in Denver now, works for a logistics company out there, doing very well for herself—she sent me one of those fancy wood pellet smokers for my birthday. It's one of those big heavy ones with the digital thermostats and the Wi-Fi connection built right into the hopper. Now, I have been a charcoal man my entire life. Just standard briquettes, a metal chimney starter, and maybe some soaked hickory chips if I was feeling ambitious on a holiday weekend. So this whole electronic, computerized smoker thing was completely new territory for me. \n\nBut I tell you what, I figured it out without a hitch. I tried reading the manual at first, though naturally my mind wandered off a few times just like we were talking about earlier, but then I went on the computer and found these instructional videos. There is this fella on there from Texas who explains the whole setup process. I had to learn how to prime the auger, how to clear out the fire pot, and how to pair the grill's computer to the internet router in the house. Which, let me tell you, our router is all the way in the front office, so I actually had to go down to the electronics store and buy a signal extender just to get the Wi-Fi to reach out to the back patio. I ended up plugging it into the outlet right behind my wife's rhododendrons. \n\nAnyway, I learned that entire system in a single afternoon. I smoked a nine-pound pork shoulder the very next day. Comprehending how a new piece of machinery works, or picking up a new skill, or even figuring out the new spreadsheet software they started using for the church finances—that hasn't changed a bit. My brain is perfectly capable of grasping new concepts and holding onto them once I actually get into the rhythm of doing it. It really is just that drifting issue, the part where I just stop absorbing the words right in front of me. But if you are asking if my overall ability to learn has gone downhill, I would have to give you a firm no on that one. I can still learn anything I set my mind to.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it difficult to remember how to do things you've done many times before, like routine chores or hobbies?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. No, not at all. The routines are... well, they're practically baked into my bones at this point. I don't have any trouble remembering how to do the things I've always done. \n\nTake the lawn care, for instance. I’ve got a quarter-acre lot, mostly Bermuda grass, which, let me tell you, can be a real nightmare if you don't stay right on top of it. I’ve been mowing that exact same lawn since we moved in. Every Tuesday morning, 8:00 AM sharp—well, unless it’s raining, of course, or if the morning dew is still too heavy, because you never want to cut wet grass, it just clumps up terribly and dulls the blade. But I go out to the shed, I pull out my Toro push mower. It’s a Recycler series, 22-inch deck, going on twelve years old now, and I know exactly how to maintain it without a second thought. I know it takes exactly 18 ounces of SAE 30 motor oil, I know to pop off the spark plug wire before I tip it over, and I know to use this old wooden paint stirrer I keep on the top shelf to scrape the dried clippings out from under the deck so the metal doesn't rust. It's just muscle memory. I could probably do the whole maintenance routine blindfolded. \n\nAnd it’s the exact same way with my hobbies. I tie my own flies for fly fishing, have since I took a class at the community college back in my twenties. Now, tying a Parachute Adams or an Elk Hair Caddis, that requires remembering a very specific, delicate sequence of steps. You have to wrap the thread, tie in the tail, dub the body, wrap the hackle... it’s a whole intricate process. But when I sit down at my vise down in the basement—I have this little corner set up next to the water heater with a nice daylight lamp—my hands just know exactly what to do. I don't need to look at a manual or pull up one of those internet videos I mentioned earlier. The knowledge is just right there, ready to go. \n\nSo, no, I never walk up to the washing machine and forget which cycle to use, or sit down at my workbench and forget how to operate my tools. The everyday chores and the old hobbies are completely untouched. Now, I know I just mentioned that I feel terrible when my wife gets frustrated with me about my cousin Gary's schedule—and that's true, it bothers me a great deal when I let family down. So, if I'm reading an article... say, about the city council meeting. They've been arguing for months about putting a new traffic light over on Miller Road, which, frankly, is a terrible idea because it's just going to back up the commuter traffic all the way to the interstate bypass. Anyway, if I'm reading that article and I suddenly realize my eyes have just been scanning the words for the last three paragraphs while my brain was actually trying to remember if I have enough charcoal briquettes for the weekend... I don't get distressed. My heart doesn't race, I don't get upset. I just sort of sigh, find the last sentence I actually absorbed, and start reading it again. \n\nAnd it's the exact same thing with casual conversations. If I'm talking to my neighbor Tom—he's always leaning over the fence wanting to talk about his garden, he's got these Cherokee Purple heirloom tomatoes this year that are just massive, really impressive—but if I tune out while he's explaining his fertilizer ratio, I don't get anxious about it. I just say, 'Sorry Tom, I missed that last bit, my mind was wandering.' It's just a nuisance, having to back up the truck and try again. So, no, no anxiety or distress about the actual slipping up part. It's just a little frustrating to have to rewind, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your brain's tendency to drift away during conversations or while reading is related to your overall mood or stress levels?\n\nPatient: Mood or stress? Hmm... well, let me think about that for a minute. Honestly, no, I really don't see a connection there. I mean, I'm a pretty easygoing guy for the most part, always have been. Sure, I get a little stressed if I'm worried about mixing up those catering orders like I mentioned, but this drifting off thing? It happens even when I don't have a single care in the world.\n\nTake last Sunday, for example. It was just a gorgeous afternoon. The weather had finally broken—you know how that awful humidity we've been having just vanished overnight? Well, I was sitting in my favorite recliner in the den. It’s this old brown leather La-Z-Boy, had it for probably fifteen years, so it's just perfectly molded to my back. I had my feet up, drinking a glass of sweet tea, completely relaxed. The Braves were on the television, playing the Mets. It was the bottom of the sixth inning, tie game, beautiful sunny day down in Atlanta on the screen. I was in a fantastic mood. We had just finished a nice lunch, just some leftover pulled pork from a small job I did on Friday, put it on those little soft Hawaiian rolls with some of that vinegar coleslaw. \n\nAnyway, I’m sitting there, feeling great, absolutely zero stress in my body... and the announcer is talking about the relief pitcher's stats, and suddenly I realize I've been staring dead at the screen for who knows how long, but my brain was actually trying to figure out if I need to power-wash and re-stain the back deck before winter sets in. I completely missed a double play! My wife came in from the kitchen and asked what happened, and I had no earthly idea. \n\nSo, no, it's definitely not just when I'm stressed out or feeling down. My brain just sort of decides to go for a walk whenever it feels like it, even if I’m as relaxed as a clam at high tide. It doesn't seem to matter if I'm having the best day of the month or a frustrating one, the wandering just happens regardless.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns since you started experiencing these issues with focusing and retaining information?\n\nPatient: Sleep patterns? Let me think... no, no, I wouldn't say so. My sleep has been pretty much exactly the same for as long as I can remember. I'm a real creature of habit when it comes to bedtime. We usually start winding down around ten o'clock, right when the local news comes on. We watch Channel 5—I always prefer their meteorologist, Dave, he just seems to get the radar right more often than the folks over on Channel 9, especially when we get those weird pop-up storm fronts moving in. \n\nAnyway, by ten-thirty, I'm in the bathroom brushing my teeth. I use that Sensodyne, you know, because my dentist told me my enamel was getting a bit thin on the bottom left side, right near a crown I had put in back in '08. Then I get into bed. We actually bought a new mattress about five years ago, a Stearns & Foster, firm but with the pillow top. Got it from that big warehouse liquidation sale out on Highway 41, and let me tell you, best investment we ever made. I lay my head down on my contoured foam pillow—it's got this little dip in the middle for your neck, really supports the spine—and I am out like a light. \n\nI mean, sure, I might wake up once around three in the morning to use the restroom, but that's just part of being fifty-nine, I reckon. It's just plumbing, nothing to do with my brain drifting off during the day. Once I'm back under the covers, I'm asleep again in five minutes flat. \n\nSo, no, this whole business with me losing the thread of conversations or forgetting my cousin's schedule... it hasn't touched my sleep one bit. I still get my solid seven or eight hours every single night. My wife actually gets a little jealous about it, to be honest with you. She's a very light sleeper, always has been. If the neighbor's dog barks two doors down, or if the garbage truck comes a little too early on Thursday mornings, she's wide awake and tossing and turning. But me? I could sleep through a freight train rolling through the front yard. I've always been a good sleeper, and that hasn't changed a bit, even with all this other stuff going on with my focus.\n\nDoctor: Are you finding it difficult to maintain relationships or perform daily tasks because of this issue with absorbing information?\n\nPatient: Well, difficult... I wouldn't say my whole life is falling apart or anything drastic like that, but it is definitely causing some real friction. Take my wife, for instance. I know I brought her up earlier, about how terrible I feel when she gets frustrated with me. Well, it’s actually started causing some genuine tension at home lately, and it really boils down to my cousin Gary’s care. \n\nGary, well, he lives about fifteen minutes away from us, over in those duplexes near the old high school, and he needs a fair bit of looking after these days. He’s got this whole complicated schedule—physical therapy on Tuesdays and Thursdays at the clinic downtown, the visiting nurse comes on Wednesdays to check his vitals, and then there's his pharmacy runs. My wife will sit down at the kitchen table with the calendar and explain the week's logistics to me, you know, who is driving him where, and I’ll be sitting right there, looking right at her, nodding my head. But then Thursday rolls around and I completely forget I was supposed to have him at the clinic by two o'clock because I just didn't absorb a word of what she said. Last week she actually had to leave her garden club meeting early to rush over there and get him. So now, she’s feeling like she just can’t count on me with his care at all. And that hurts, it really does, because we’ve been married thirty-two years and we've always been a team, but she says she feels like she's managing him entirely by herself because she can't trust me to retain the schedule.\n\nAnd then with my own daily tasks... well, since I left the regular workforce, I do these small catering jobs to keep busy and bring in a little extra spending money. Nothing huge, just, you know, fifty people for a retirement party, or a family reunion down at the state park pavilions. I do a lot of barbecue, smoked briskets, potato salad, that sort of thing. But because of this issue with missing information, I’ve had to start double-checking absolutely everything I do. I'll take an order from a client over the phone, and if I don't write it down the exact second they say it, I lose the details. \n\nI had a scare last month where I almost showed up to a fiftieth anniversary party with three trays of spicy jalapeño poppers instead of the mild stuffed mushrooms they specifically asked for. I had completely tuned out when the lady was explaining her husband's terrible heartburn issues. I actually had to throw out a whole batch of prep work and redo the catering tasks the morning of the event. So now, I'm constantly having to double-check my ingredient lists, or call folks back to confirm their side dishes, or redo prep work in the kitchen just so these small jobs don't get mixed up. It hasn't completely derailed my little business, but it's a whole lot of extra work, and I hate feeling like I'm always one wandering thought away from ruining someone's special event.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel any emotional distress when you realize you've missed important information in a conversation or while reading?\n\nPatient: Emotional distress? Well, let me think on that word for a second. Distress... no, I really wouldn't use a heavy word like that. Like I said earlier, I’m a pretty easygoing fellow. \n\nTake reading, for example. I like to read a fair bit of history, mostly Civil War stuff or biographies. Just last Tuesday, I was out on the back patio. We have this nice little screened-in area my brother-in-law and I built back in '14. It keeps the mosquitoes out, which have been just absolutely terrible this year with all the late spring rain we had. Anyway, I was sitting out there on the glider, reading this big thick biography on Ulysses S. Grant that I picked up at a secondhand bookstore over in Marietta. Great little store, by the way, smells exactly like old paper and coffee, run by this older gentleman named Arthur who always remembers my name. \n\nSo, I’m reading along, and suddenly I realize my eyes have scanned down about four whole pages, but my brain was completely somewhere else—probably thinking about a new dry rub for my briskets or something. I had absolutely no earthly idea what had just happened at the Siege of Vicksburg. Now, did I feel distressed about it? Not at all. I just sort of chuckled to myself, shook my head, and put my bookmark in. It’s this nice little tooled leather bookmark my daughter brought back for me when she studied abroad in Florence, Italy, back in her junior year of college. I don't see any sense in getting my blood pressure up over having to reread a page or asking someone to repeat a story. Life's too short to get distressed over every little wandering thought, wouldn't you agree?\n\nDoctor: Do you think your brain's tendency to drift away could be related to any underlying medical or psychological conditions that you're aware of?\n\nPatient: Medical conditions? Gosh, I really don't think so. I mean, I'm generally in pretty good shape for a guy staring down sixty. I go see my primary care doctor, Dr. Aris—he’s got that practice right next to the old post office, the one with the nice brick front and the big oak tree out by the sidewalk? Anyway, I go see him every single year for my annual physical like clockwork. \n\nI just had my last one done back in, oh, it must have been late September, because I remember it was right before the big autumn festival down at the town square where I was doing a huge order of pulled pork sliders. Dr. Aris ran all the usual blood work, checked the cholesterol, the blood sugar, the whole nine yards. He told me my triglycerides were just a hair elevated, but he said that’s nothing to lose sleep over, just maybe told me to cut back on the mayonnaise in the potato salad I make for my catering gigs. My blood pressure is right as rain, usually sitting around 120 over 80, which he says is fantastic for my age. I do take a little daily multivitamin, one of those men’s 50-plus ones, and a glucosamine supplement for my left knee—I tweaked it playing softball in a church league about fifteen years ago, and it still acts up a little when a cold front moves in. My ticker is strong, lungs are clear. \n\nAnd as for the psychological side of things... well, I’ve never really had any trouble in that department. I’m not a depressed sort of fellow, I don’t get anxious or have panic attacks or anything heavy like that. Like I was saying earlier, I’m a pretty easygoing guy, always have been. Now, my older brother, he had some trouble with his nerves back in the late nineties after he got laid off from the auto plant, but he got that all sorted out after a while. For me, though? Never had a diagnosis of any kind. \n\nSo, honestly, I don't have the faintest idea if this drifting off is tied to anything else, because as far as I know, my health record is completely clean. Remembering things from before? Gosh, well... let me think back. You know, I've always been a bit of a storyteller, and I can usually pull up a memory from way back when without too much trouble. 

Like, I can remember clear as day the time my dad took me to my first major league baseball game. It was 1974, Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium, before they tore it down and built Turner Field. Hank Aaron hit a home run that day—not *the* home run, you know, not the 715th that broke Babe Ruth's record, that was a few months earlier, but it was still a beauty right over the left-field wall. I was eating a hot dog with extra mustard, and I remember the mustard dripped right down onto my brand new white sneakers. My mother was absolutely fit to be tied when we got home, scrubbing those shoes with an old toothbrush and some kind of strong-smelling bleach solution out on the back porch. 

And I can remember high school, too. I played tuba in the marching band. We had these awful, heavy wool uniforms that were just miserable in the Georgia heat during early September football games. I remember marching in the homecoming parade my senior year, right down Main Street, past the old hardware store that used to be where the new pharmacy is now. I can still picture the exact shade of blue on the banner the cheerleaders were carrying ahead of us. 

Even my early days working—before I got into the catering and the barbecue, I worked for a spell at a local printing press right after I took a few classes at the community college. I can remember the smell of the ink, the loud clanking of the Heidelberg presses, and the way the paper dust used to settle on everything by the end of the shift. I can even remember the name of my shift supervisor, a gruff fellow named Dale who always had a half-chewed cigar tucked behind his ear. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I have any trouble remembering things from before this whole drifting off business started getting noticeable. My long-term memory seems to be just fine, sharp as a tack for the most part. I can recall all those old stories and events without a hitch. It's really just the present moment, the right-here-and-now stuff, like reading that biography or listening to Bob talk about his lawn fertilizer, where my brain decides to take a little unscheduled detour. The old memories, they're all still filed away perfectly in the cabinets up there!
